topics.title: Movement, locomotion and types of movement

learn.hook: When you blink, you move but stay in place. When you run a 100 m dash, you move and change location. Only one of them is locomotion.
points: Movement is a significant feature of living beings: streaming of protoplasm in Amoeba, movement of cilia, flagella and tentacles, and in humans movement of limbs, jaws, eyelids and tongue.
Locomotion is voluntary movement that results in a change of place or location (walking, running, climbing, flying, swimming). All locomotions are movements, but all movements are not locomotions.

The same structures can serve both: Paramoecium uses cilia to move food through the cytopharynx and for locomotion; Hydra uses tentacles to capture prey and to move; we use limbs for posture changes and locomotion.

Human cells show three main movements. Amoeboid movement: macrophages and leucocytes move by pseudopodia formed by protoplasmic streaming; cytoskeletal microfilaments are involved. Ciliary movement: in tubular organs lined by ciliated epithelium, e.g. cilia in the trachea remove dust, and cilia help ova pass through the female reproductive tract.
Muscular movement: movement of limbs, jaws and tongue uses the contractile property of muscles. Locomotion needs perfectly coordinated activity of the muscular, skeletal and neural systems.

example.q: Classify: (a) a WBC squeezing through a capillary, (b) dust being swept up the trachea, (c) chewing food.
steps: (a) Pseudopodia by protoplasmic streaming: amoeboid movement.
(b) Coordinated beating of cilia: ciliary movement.
(c) Jaw muscles contracting: muscular movement.

learn.reallife: Neeraj Chopra's javelin throw is a perfect example of muscular, skeletal and neural systems working in precise coordination.

learn.hook: About 40 to 50% of your body weight is muscle. That's like a 60 kg student carrying 24 to 30 kg of muscle everywhere.
points: Muscle is a specialised tissue of mesodermal origin, contributing about 40 to 50% of an adult human's body weight.
Special properties of muscle: excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity.
Skeletal muscles: closely associated with skeletal components; striped (striated) under the microscope; under voluntary control (voluntary muscles); mainly for locomotion and posture changes.

Visceral muscles: in the inner walls of hollow visceral organs such as the alimentary canal and reproductive tract; no striations (smooth or non-striated); involuntary; help move food through the gut and gametes through the genital tract.
Cardiac muscles: muscles of the heart; many cells assemble in a branching pattern; striated but involuntary, since the nervous system does not control them directly.

example.q: A 60 kg adult has muscles making up 45% of body weight. What is the mass of muscle?
steps: Muscle mass = 45% of 60 kg.

learn.reallife: Gym trainers in Indian cities train skeletal (voluntary) muscles, but no amount of willpower can directly speed up your cardiac or gut muscles.

topics.title: Structure of skeletal muscle and the sarcomere

learn.hook: Under a microscope, a muscle fibre looks like a barcode of light and dark stripes. Each stripe pattern repeats in tiny units called sarcomeres.
points: A skeletal muscle is made of bundles called fascicles held together by a collagenous connective tissue layer, the fascia. Each fascicle contains many muscle fibres.

Each muscle fibre is lined by the sarcolemma (plasma membrane) enclosing the sarcoplasm; it has many nuclei, so it is a syncytium. Its sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium ions. The sarcoplasm has many parallel myofibrils (myofilaments).
Myofibrils show alternate light and dark bands due to actin and myosin. The light I band (isotropic) contains actin (thin filaments); the dark A band (anisotropic) contains myosin (thick filaments).
An elastic fibre, the Z line, bisects each I band; thin filaments are attached to it. Thick filaments are held together in the middle of the A band by the M line.

The sarcomere, the portion between two successive Z lines, is the functional unit of contraction. At rest, thin filaments partially overlap the ends of thick filaments; the central part of the thick filaments not overlapped is the H zone.

example.q: Label the bands and lines from one Z line to the next in a resting sarcomere.
steps: Z line, then half an I band (actin only).
The A band (myosin) begins; at its centre is the H zone, bisected by the M line.
The A band ends, then half an I band, then the next Z line.
example.answer: Z line → ½ I band → A band (with H zone and M line) → ½ I band → Z line

learn.reallife: Sports physiologists at the National Institute of Sports, Patiala, study muscle biopsies to understand how training changes muscle fibres.

learn.hook: Myosin heads are tiny motors that grab actin, pull and let go, hundreds of times a second, powered by ATP.
points: Each actin (thin) filament has two F (filamentous) actins helically wound around each other; each F actin is a polymer of G (globular) actin monomers.
Two filaments of tropomyosin run close to the F actins along their length.
The complex protein troponin is distributed at regular intervals on tropomyosin. At rest, a subunit of troponin masks the active binding sites for myosin on actin.

Each myosin (thick) filament is a polymer of many monomers called meromyosins. Each meromyosin has a globular head with a short arm, the heavy meromyosin (HMM), and a tail, the light meromyosin (LMM).

The HMM (head and short arm) projects outwards at regular distances and angles from the thick filament as a cross arm. The globular head is an active ATPase enzyme with binding sites for ATP and active sites for actin.

example.q: Why can a resting muscle not contract even if ATP is present?
steps: Myosin heads need to bind actin to form cross bridges.
At rest, a troponin subunit masks the myosin-binding sites on actin.
Until Ca²⁺ removes this masking, cross bridges cannot form.
example.answer: Troponin masks the actin sites until Ca²⁺ arrives.

learn.reallife: Muscle cramps after heavy training at Indian sports academies are linked to problems in this actin-myosin cycle and in calcium and energy supply.

topics.title: Mechanism of muscle contraction: the sliding filament theory

learn.hook: When you lift your school bag, millions of thin filaments slide over thick ones. The filaments themselves don't get shorter at all.
points: Sliding filament theory: a muscle fibre contracts by the sliding of thin filaments over thick filaments.

A signal from the CNS travels via a motor neuron to the neuromuscular junction (motor end plate), releasing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, which generates an action potential in the sarcolemma. It spreads through the fibre and causes release of Ca²⁺ into the sarcoplasm.

Ca²⁺ binds a subunit of troponin, unmasking the active sites on actin. Using energy from ATP hydrolysis, the myosin head binds actin to form a cross bridge and pulls the actin towards the centre of the A band. The Z lines are pulled inward, shortening the sarcomere.

During contraction, the I bands shorten (and the H zone narrows), while the A bands keep their length. Myosin releases ADP and Pi and goes back to its relaxed state; a new ATP binds, breaking the cross bridge; the cycle repeats.
When Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic cisternae, actin sites are masked again and the Z lines return to their original positions: relaxation.

example.q: Put the events of muscle contraction in order, from the nerve signal to sarcomere shortening.
steps: Motor neuron signal reaches the neuromuscular junction; acetylcholine is released.
Action potential spreads in the sarcolemma; Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Ca²⁺ binds troponin, exposing actin sites.
Myosin heads form cross bridges using ATP energy and pull actin inward; the sarcomere shortens.
example.answer: Signal → acetylcholine → action potential → Ca²⁺ release → troponin binding → cross bridges → sliding

learn.reallife: Indian weightlifter Mirabai Chanu's lifts depend on rapid, repeated cross-bridge cycles in her muscles, each powered by ATP.

topics.title: Motor units, fatigue, and red versus white fibres

learn.hook: Marathon runners and sprinters train very different muscles. One relies on oxygen-loving red fibres, the other on quick white fibres.
points: A motor neuron together with the muscle fibres connected to it forms a motor unit.
Reaction time of fibres varies in different muscles.
Repeated activation of muscles can cause accumulation of lactic acid from anaerobic breakdown of glycogen, causing fatigue.
Red fibres: high content of the red, oxygen-storing pigment myoglobin; plenty of mitochondria using stored O₂ for ATP; called aerobic muscles.
White fibres: very little myoglobin, so pale; few mitochondria but a large amount of sarcoplasmic reticulum; depend on anaerobic processes for energy.

example.q: A muscle fibre has lots of myoglobin and mitochondria. Classify it and say how it gets energy.
steps: High myoglobin gives a red colour.
Many mitochondria use stored oxygen.
So it is a red, aerobic fibre.

learn.reallife: Marathon runners at events like the Mumbai Marathon rely on red, aerobic fibres for endurance, while 100 m sprinters rely more on white fibres for short bursts.

topics.title: The skeleton: axial skeleton, skull and vertebral column

learn.hook: A newborn has about 300 bones, but many fuse, leaving an adult with 206. Eighty of them run along your body's central axis.
points: The skeletal system is a framework of bones and a few cartilages. Bone has a very hard matrix due to calcium salts; cartilage has a slightly pliable matrix due to chondroitin salts. Adults have 206 bones, grouped into axial and appendicular skeletons.
The axial skeleton has 80 bones along the main axis: skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs.

Skull: 22 bones: 8 cranial bones forming the cranium that protects the brain, and 14 facial bones. A U-shaped hyoid bone at the base of the buccal cavity and three ear ossicles in each middle ear (malleus, incus, stapes) are also included. The skull joins the vertebral column by two occipital condyles (dicondylic skull).

Vertebral column: 26 serially arranged vertebrae, dorsally placed. Each vertebra has a central neural canal for the spinal cord. The first vertebra, the atlas, articulates with the occipital condyles.

Regions: cervical 7, thoracic 12, lumbar 5, sacral 1 (fused), coccygeal 1 (fused). Almost all mammals, including humans, have 7 cervical vertebrae. The column protects the spinal cord, supports the head and anchors the ribs and back muscles.

example.q: Show that the axial skeleton has 80 bones.
steps: Skull 22 + hyoid 1 + ear ossicles 6 (3 × 2) = 29.
Vertebrae 26 + sternum 1 + ribs 24 (12 pairs) = 51.

learn.reallife: A giraffe's long neck and your neck have the same number of cervical vertebrae: seven. Orthopaedic surgeons in India often treat cervical spondylosis in desk workers.

topics.title: Ribs, limbs and girdles: the appendicular skeleton

learn.hook: Each of your hands and feet holds 14 phalanges. Count your finger joints and you'll see why.
points: The sternum is a flat bone on the ventral midline of the thorax. There are 12 pairs of ribs; each is a thin flat bone joined dorsally to the vertebral column and ventrally to the sternum, with two articulation surfaces at its dorsal end (bicephalic).

Ribs 1 to 7 (true ribs) attach dorsally to thoracic vertebrae and ventrally to the sternum by hyaline cartilage. Ribs 8, 9, 10 (vertebrochondral or false ribs) join the 7th rib by hyaline cartilage. Ribs 11 and 12 (floating ribs) are not connected ventrally. Thoracic vertebrae, ribs and sternum form the rib cage.

Appendicular skeleton (126 bones): limbs and girdles. Each limb has 30 bones. Forelimb: humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges. Hind limb: femur (longest bone), tibia, fibula, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges and the patella (knee cap).

Pectoral girdle: each half has a clavicle (collar bone) and a scapula. The scapula is a large triangular flat bone on the dorsal thorax between the 2nd and 7th ribs; its spine projects as the acromion, with which the clavicle articulates. Below the acromion, the glenoid cavity articulates with the head of the humerus to form the shoulder joint.

Pelvic girdle: two coxal bones, each formed by fusion of ilium, ischium and pubis. At their fusion is the acetabulum, where the thigh bone articulates. The two halves meet ventrally at the pubic symphysis, containing fibrous cartilage.

example.q: Show that one forelimb has 30 bones.
steps: Humerus 1 + radius 1 + ulna 1 = 3.
Carpals 8 + metacarpals 5 + phalanges 14 = 27.

learn.reallife: Cricketers often fracture phalanges or metacarpals while fielding; orthopaedic doctors in India read X-rays using exactly these bone names.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to count bones in his arm and leg and sort his ribs. Explain the rib cage, limbs and girdles!

teach.nudge: Good! How many bones are in one limb, and what are true, false and floating ribs?

learn.hook: Your shoulder can swing a cricket bat in a full circle, but your knee only bends one way. Different joints, different jobs.
points: Joints are points of contact between bones, or between bones and cartilages. They are essential for all movements of bony parts. The force from muscles acts through the joint, which works as a fulcrum.
Fibrous joints do not allow any movement, e.g. flat skull bones fused end to end by dense fibrous connective tissue as sutures, forming the cranium.
Cartilaginous joints join bones with cartilage and allow limited movement, e.g. the joints between adjacent vertebrae.
Synovial joints have a fluid-filled synovial cavity between the articulating surfaces, allowing considerable movement; they help in locomotion and many other movements.
Types of synovial joints: ball and socket (humerus and pectoral girdle), hinge (knee), pivot (atlas and axis), gliding (between carpals), saddle (between carpal and metacarpal of the thumb).

example.q: Which joint lets you turn your head to say 'no', and which type is it?
steps: Turning the head is rotation around the neck's axis.
This happens between the atlas and the axis.
It is a pivot joint, a type of synovial joint.
example.answer: The atlas-axis joint, a pivot (synovial) joint.

learn.reallife: Bharatanatyam dancers use the full range of ball and socket joints at the shoulders and hips, while the knees act as hinges.

quiz.q: The joint between the humerus and the pectoral girdle is a:
quiz.explain: It allows movement in many directions.

quiz.q: The knee joint is an example of a:
quiz.explain: It bends mainly in one plane.

quiz.q: Joints between adjacent vertebrae are:
quiz.explain: Cartilage joins the vertebrae and allows limited movement.

quiz.q: Skull bones are joined by:
quiz.explain: Sutures allow no movement.

quiz.q: The joint between the carpal and metacarpal of the thumb is a:
quiz.explain: This saddle joint lets the thumb move widely.

quiz.q: Synovial joints are characterised by:
quiz.explain: The cavity allows considerable movement.
options: Dense fibrous tissue with no movement
A fluid-filled synovial cavity between articulating surfaces
Cartilage that allows only limited movement

quiz.q: Joints between carpals are:
quiz.explain: Carpals slide over each other.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A joint acts as a fulcrum during movement. Reason (R): The force generated by muscles is used to move bones through joints.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; muscles apply force and the joint is the pivot point.
quiz.mistake: Does not link force with the fulcrum role

teach.ask: Gappu swings a bat and bends his knee. Explain the types of joints and give examples!
teach.praise: Tweet! Fixed sutures, slightly movable vertebrae, and free-moving synovial joints!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the three types of joints, and give one example of each synovial type?

topics.title: Disorders of the muscular and skeletal system

learn.hook: Many elderly women in India break a wrist or hip from a minor fall. A silent bone disease called osteoporosis is often the cause.
points: Myasthenia gravis: an autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigue, weakening and paralysis of skeletal muscle.
Muscular dystrophy: progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle, mostly due to a genetic disorder.
Tetany: rapid spasms (wild contractions) in muscle due to low Ca²⁺ in body fluid.
Arthritis: inflammation of joints. Gout: inflammation of joints due to accumulation of uric acid crystals.
Osteoporosis: an age-related disorder with decreased bone mass and higher chances of fractures; decreased levels of oestrogen are a common cause.

example.q: A patient has painful swollen joints, and tests show uric acid crystals in them. Name the disorder.
steps: Joint inflammation suggests arthritis-type disorders.
Uric acid crystals in joints specifically indicate gout.

learn.reallife: Calcium and vitamin D intake and weight-bearing exercise are promoted in India to reduce osteoporosis, especially after menopause.

quiz.q: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder affecting the:
quiz.explain: It causes fatigue, weakness and paralysis of skeletal muscle.

quiz.q: Rapid spasms in muscle due to low Ca²⁺ in body fluid is:
quiz.explain: Low calcium causes tetany.

quiz.q: Accumulation of uric acid crystals in joints causes:
quiz.explain: Gout is joint inflammation from uric acid crystals.

quiz.q: A common cause of osteoporosis is:
quiz.explain: Age-related loss of oestrogen reduces bone mass.

quiz.q: Muscular dystrophy is mostly due to:
quiz.explain: It is progressive and mostly genetic.

quiz.q: Inflammation of joints is called:
quiz.explain: Arthr- means joint, -itis means inflammation.

quiz.q: Osteoporosis increases the chance of:
quiz.explain: Low bone mass makes bones fragile.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Low calcium in body fluids can cause rapid muscle spasms. Reason (R): Gout is caused by low Ca²⁺ in body fluids.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true: this condition is tetany. R is false: gout is joint inflammation caused by accumulation of uric acid crystals, not by low calcium.
quiz.mistake: Accepts the reason without checking it against the facts

teach.ask: Gappu's grandmother broke her wrist in a small fall, and his uncle has swollen toes. Explain the muscle and bone disorders!
teach.praise: Chirp! Fragile bones, swollen joints and weak muscles each have a cause. Knowledge is the first cure!
teach.nudge: Good! What causes gout, tetany and osteoporosis?
